CERTIORARI -- SUMMARY DISPOSITIONS
25-901 GARCIA, BENANCIO V. HOBBS, SEC. OF STATE WA, ET AL.
25-918 TREVINO, JOSE A., ET AL. V. HOBBS, SEC. OF STATE WA, ET AL.
The petitions for writs of certiorari are granted. The
judgments are vacated, and the cases are remanded to the United
States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit for further
consideration in light of Louisiana v. Callais, 608 U. S. 85
(2026).
25-7462 WHITEHEAD, LAMOR V. UNITED STATES
The motion of petitioner for leave to proceed in forma
pauperis and the petition for a writ of certiorari are granted.
The judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded to the United
States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit for further
consideration in light of Abouammo v. United States, 608 U. S.
597 (2026).
25-7532 SNIPE, JULIAN V. UNITED STATES
The motion of petitioner for leave to proceed in forma
pauperis and the petition for a writ of certiorari are granted.
The judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded to the United
States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit for further
consideration in light of Hunter v. United States, 608 U. S. 713
(2026).

States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit for further
consideration in light of Hunter v. United States, 608 U. S. 713
(2026).

consideration in light of Hunter v. United States, 608 U. S. 713
(2026).

1Cite as: 610 U. S. ____ (2026)
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J.
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
STEVEN RICHARD MULKEY v. ALABAMA
ON PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE
COURT OF CRIMINAL APPEALS OF ALABAMA
No. 25–7499. Decided October 5, 2026
The petition for a writ of certiorari is denied.
Statement of JUSTICE SOTOMAYOR respecting the denial
of certiorari.
The right to an impartial jury, embedded both in the
Sixth Amendment and the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due
Process Clause, is fundamental to our system of justice. See
Gray v. Mississippi, 481 U. S. 648, 657 (1987); Gomez v.
United States, 490 U. S. 858, 876 (1989). It is the role of a
judge to protect, not endanger, that impartiality. In this
case, during jury selection for a capital murder trial, the
trial judge held a potential juror in contempt for being 30
minutes late to court and ordered him arrested. Those or-
ders were issued in front of the remaining pool of potential
jurors.
After the judge ordered the tardy juror arrested, two po-
tential jurors, who were questioned individually during
voir dire, expressed fear of sharing their views about the
case. One potential juror asked, after the judge inquired
about his unwillingness to recommend the death penalty,
“Will I be charged or thrown in jail?” 6 Record 409. An-
other, after being asked whether he was willing to consider
mitigating factors in deciding whether to recommend a
death sentence, stated: “Well, I kind of based [my opinion]
on what the Judge told me, because I don’t want to get in
trouble for my beliefs.” 7 id., at 482. Although the judge
assured these jurors that they would not be punished for
sharing their views, this assurance was given during the
individual questioning and not in the presence of the rest of
2 MULKEY v. ALABAMA
Statement of SOTOMAYOR, J.
the jury pool. It is unknown how many other potential ju-
rors felt similarly but did not share their fear because they
were not called for individual questioning.
This case comes to us on plain-error review because no
objection to the judge’s conduct was raised below. Because
that posture limits the scope of our review, I concur in the
Court’s denial of certiorari. I write, however, to highlight
that this case provides an example of why judges should re-
strain themselves from conducting any proceedings that are
collateral to the trial in front of a jury.
The record here amply demonstrates how a judge’s con-
duct can have a profoundly negative impact on members of
the jury pool. Such conduct may affect not only what poten-
tial jurors are willing to say in front of the judge, but also
whether they will apply their independent judgment in-
stead of following what they perceive the judge may person-
ally think. See, e.g., Starr v. United States, 153 U. S. 614,
626 (1894). If potential jurors are not comfortable express-
ing their own views, voir dire’s “critical function” of identi-
fying and removing prospective jurors who cannot be im-
partial is undermined. Rosales-Lopez v. United States, 451
U. S. 182, 188 (1981) (plurality opinion). “The influence of
the voir dire process,” moreover, “may persist through the
whole course of the trial proceedings.” Powers v. Ohio, 499
U. S. 400, 412 (1991). This danger is especially acute in a
capital case such as this one, where the defendant’s life
hangs in the balance. To guard against it, judges should
limit exposing a jury to collateral proceedings, particularly
when those proceedings might frighten or intimidate the
jury.
